content: 1. The initial meeting of the multi-stakeholder working group should be convened to finalize the terms of reference, discuss and agree on governance structures, and establish mechanisms for accountability and responsibility. This step is critical for initiating the legal framework. 2. The structure and operational mechanisms of the multi-stakeholder working group must be formalized. The WHO country office may participate as either a core or additional member to provide technical support and guidance. Additional members, ideally including donors, should be incorporated to support both the catalytic first year and the establishment of a sustainable budget. A detailed cost roadmap should also be developed. 3. The multi-stakeholder working group should appoint a secretariat to oversee the various activities. This responsibility will likely fall under the Ministry of Health, depending on the country’s existing health workforce infrastructure, such as registries, observatories, or national accounts frameworks. 4. A technical working group, composed of members and co-opted experts from the multi-stakeholder group, should be designated to collect and analyze data and conduct the scoping analysis outlined in Step 3. 5. The multi-stakeholder working group must identify and agree on key policy questions to be addressed through scoping and the compilation and analysis of health workforce data. Available resources and references should be consulted to guide this process. 6. During the scoping and planning phase, the technical working group will map existing data and data systems within the country and develop a plan for additional health workforce data collection. Core indicators should be defined based on the key policy questions identified in Step 2 before data collection begins. 7. The hierarchy and availability of data sources should be assessed to prioritize those that best address the policy questions and meet the requirements of the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA). This analysis will identify gaps in data sources that require targeted data collection efforts in subsequent steps. 8. The scoping analysis should also review potential discrepancies in information when the same indicator is derived from multiple sources. A prioritization of sources should be established based on accuracy, completeness, and efficiency of data collection. 9. While mapping data sources, the multi-stakeholder working group should develop a global dissemination plan for health workforce data. A business plan should also be created to outline data collection strategies and propose new data capture methods as needed. The size of the business plan will depend on available funding and the volume of data to be collected. 10. The business plan should define core funding, human resources, infrastructure, and technology requirements for data processing, as well as potential sources of national and external catalytic funding. It should also describe the financial administration process and risk evaluation. 11. The communication and business plans could be developed during the multi-stakeholder working group meeting outlined in Step 2, depending on the country’s existing framework. 12. The NHWA process should begin with an evaluation of the current state of the health workforce information system in the country. This evaluation will identify available data and potential actions to address knowledge gaps. 13. A national and global dissemination plan for the NHWA should be developed, and a business plan should be defined to support the Sustainable Development Goals and improve the completeness of NHWA indicator data. 14. The scoping analysis document should provide an overview of the current state of health workforce data in the country, identify data gaps, and outline information sources across stakeholders. 15. A costing analysis for the first year of NHWA implementation should be completed, and a plan for a regular rolling budget should be defined, including potential donors and funding sources. 16. The technical working group established in Step 2 should be supplemented with external experts to conduct the scoping analysis on the current state of health workforce data and sources, using the NHWA to identify topics to be addressed. 17. Consultations with health bodies, academics, economists, and other stakeholders should be organized to identify additional data sources of interest, such as surveys and research projects. 18. The technical working group should explore methods to maintain, process, and integrate data from various sources, including IT compatibility and strategies for data exchange. Stakeholder IT departments may provide assistance. 19. The NHWA online data platform includes a maturity assessment that should be used to summarize available indicators. 20. An analysis plan should be prepared to address policy questions posed by the multi-stakeholder working group in Step 2, based on identified data sources and projects. 21. A public dissemination plan for the scoping analysis and results of health workforce data collection and analysis should be prepared, including national-level recommendations. International dissemination can utilize existing channels such as WHO regional offices. 22. Academic institutions should be involved to stimulate and encourage new research activities on health workforce issues in the country. 23. The multi-stakeholder coordination working group should meet to define the costing for the first year of implementation and plan the establishment of a regular rolling budget. 24. Understanding the legal framework in the country and its impact on health workforce data collection, analysis, and use is essential. This step ensures that NHWA activities led by the multi-stakeholder working group can operate legally. 25. Legal requirements for data gathering, management, confidentiality, ownership, and exchange must be addressed early in the process to avoid wasted time and resources. 26. Reporting policies should align with legal requirements and authorizations for health workforce data exchange and sharing. The secretariat, with the help of responsible bodies, will ensure all necessary authorizations and clearances are obtained. 27. The secretariat will establish a process for reporting and correcting any breaches during data exchange. 28. The terms of reference and regulations for governance, defined in Step 2, should align with the national legal environment. All legal aspects of data gathering and exchange, including anonymization and removal of sensitive information, must be formalized. 29. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) should be defined and implemented, including a mitigation plan for potential breaches during data exchange. 30. The secretariat should identify all national bodies relevant to stakeholders in the working group, particularly those responsible for ethics, data confidentiality, anonymization, and data exchange. 31. Legal advice should be sought to ensure alignment with national regulations and to establish a legal framework covering governance rules outlined in Step 2. A legal advisor may be invited to participate in the multi-stakeholder working group. 32. Institutions and bodies with access to data should be identified, and SOPs should be established for access to each type of required data, considering the source, confidentiality level, and aggregation. 33. SOPs should address the legal aspects of disseminating results from the NHWA platform, national information systems, and technical documents to ensure broad public access to information. 34. SOPs should also include processes for identifying, reporting, and correcting any data breaches during data gathering, exchange, and reporting. 35. Data collection and management from multiple sources should follow the plan defined in Step 3 to answer key policy questions and identify potential data gaps. 36. The technical working group will define quality and eligibility criteria and harmonize data for use in the NHWA. Triangulation through comparison and hierarchy of data sources should be established for cases with multiple sources for the same indicator. 37. The NHWA platform hosted by WHO enables standardized data and provides tools for analysis and visualization. 38. A process document describing data sources and flows across stakeholders, with metadata, should be developed, defining legal requirements for data access and sharing. 39. The final list of data sources for the NHWA should be prepared, defining a set of data quality standards. Data on NHWA indicators should be centralized by the secretariat. 40. The technical working group should provide a quality assessment of data sources identified in the scoping analysis, highlighting potential data gaps to guide the stakeholder working group. 41. A working document describing harmonized data definitions and sources should be developed, evaluating the IT environment, database, and interoperability. 42. The secretariat should supervise NHWA data collection through a formal network of focal points and ensure centralization of aggregated NHWA data. 43. Each data provider should collect raw data, perform data aggregation, and produce a summary of indicators to transfer to the secretariat. Existing platforms for data sharing in the country or the NHWA online platform can be used for this purpose. 44. A cost/value evaluation could assist stakeholders in reviewing information before commissioning data. 45. Validation of data and information produced is essential. The technical working group will translate the data to help the multi-stakeholder working group interpret findings and develop recommendations based on analyses. 46. The multi-stakeholder working group will define key messages for dissemination to decision-makers, the general public, and academia. 47. Political and technical validation of the NHWA process will be formalized by the multi-stakeholder working group to make policy recommendations and outline actions for the next round of data collection. 48. Guides and briefings containing key health workforce messages for decision-makers, the public, and academia will be prepared for dissemination. 49. A report on the state of health workforce data, highlighting data quality, gaps, and actions for improvement, will be developed, adopted, and produced. 50. If early access to data is legally and practically possible, a national workshop with external expertise on the health workforce could support the NHWA process.
